summary: Describes a framework for preparing Unicode text strings so that input and comparison behave sensibly for users worldwide. It is useful for identifiers, names and internationalized domain names, but does not itself say how protocols should prepare strings; individual protocols define profiles. It was replaced by RFC 7564.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people can type what looks like the same name and have the computer store different characters, so a lookup fails. This RFC describes a way to clean up text before it is used as an identifier: delete the characters that carry no meaning, make upper and lower case match, and reject the characters that would confuse the display.

subtitle: A framework for preparing Unicode text so that strings typed by different people compare equal.

tldr.problem: Text typed on different systems can look identical but be built from different characters, so a protocol that compares strings character by character can report that two names are different when the users meant the same name.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines four ordered steps: map characters to other characters or delete them, optionally normalize the result to Unicode form KC, reject prohibited characters, and check right-to-left text.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3454 was obsoleted by RFC 7564, which sets out the PRECIS framework for preparing, enforcing and comparing internationalized strings in application protocols. This document is the earlier stringprep framework, and it does not say how any protocol should use it: each protocol must define a profile, and those profiles are registered with IANA.

facts.label: Mapping tables
facts.value: B.2 with normalization form KC, B.3 without

today: RFC 3454 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 7564, which sets out the PRECIS framework for preparing, enforcing and comparing internationalized strings in application protocols, so this document should be read as the earlier version of the stringprep rules. The document itself notes that it applies to Unicode version 3.2 and does not automatically apply to later versions of Unicode.

sections.title: Why Text Needs Preparing
sections.content:
Application programs can display text in many different ways, and a user can enter text into an application program in a myriad of fashions. Internationalized text, that is, text that is not restricted to the narrow set of US-ASCII characters, has many input and display behaviors that make it difficult to compare text in a consistent fashion.

This document specifies a framework of processing rules for Unicode text. Other protocols can create profiles of these rules, and these profiles will allow users to enter internationalized text strings in applications and have the highest chance of getting the content of the strings correct. Here, correct means that if two different people enter what they think is the same string into two different input mechanisms, the strings should match on a character-by-character basis.

The framework does not describe how data is transcoded from other character sets into Unicode. In systems that use non-Unicode character sets, the transcoding algorithm is a critical part of enabling secure and correct operation of internationalized text strings.

Profiles can also exclude characters that should not normally appear in text used in the protocol. The profile can prevent such characters by changing them to other characters, by removing them, or by causing an error if they would appear in the output. For example, because the backspace character can cause unpredictable display results, a profile can specify that a string containing a backspace character would cause an error. A profile converts a single string of input characters to a string of output characters, or returns an error if the output string would contain a prohibited character, and it cannot both emit a string and return an error.

Profiles cannot account for all of the variations that might occur or that a user might expect. In particular, a profile will not be able to account for choice of spellings in all languages for all scripts, because the number of alternative spellings is immense. Users would probably expect all spelling equivalents to be made equivalent, or none of them to be. Examples include theater against theatre, and the simplified and traditional Chinese spellings of the same name.

The stringprep protocol does not stand on its own; it has to be used by other protocols at precisely defined places in those protocols. A protocol that does string comparison as a step might specify that such comparison is done only after processing the strings with a specific profile. When two protocols that use different profiles interoperate, there may be conflict about what characters are and are not allowed in the final string, so protocol developers should strongly consider re-using existing profiles. Where developers wish to allow users as wide a range of characters as possible, they should, where possible, cause stringprep to convert characters from the input string to a canonical form instead of prohibiting them.

Although it would be easy to use the stringprep process to correct perceived mis-features or bugs in the current character standards, stringprep profiles SHOULD NOT do so. A profile can create tables different from those in the appendices of this document, but it will be an exception when they do: the intention of stringprep is to define the tables and have the profiles select among those defined tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people can type what looks like the same name and have the computer store different characters, so a lookup fails. This RFC describes a way to clean up text before it is used as an identifier: delete the characters that carry no meaning, make upper and lower case match, and reject the characters that would confuse the display.

sections.title: The Four Steps of Preparation
sections.content:
The steps for preparing strings are, in order: map, normalize, prohibit and check bidi.

Map. For each character in the input, check if it has a mapping and, if so, replace it with its mapping. Each character in the input stream MUST be checked against a mapping table. The mapping table SHOULD come from this document, although it MAY be added to or altered by the profile. For any individual character, the table MAY specify that a character be mapped to nothing, to one other character, or to a string of other characters. Mapped characters are not re-scanned during the mapping step: if character A at position X is mapped to character B, the B that is now at position X is not checked against the mapping table again.

Normalize. Possibly normalize the result of step 1 using Unicode normalization.

Prohibit. Check for any characters that are not allowed in the output. If any are found, return an error.

Check bidi. Possibly check for right-to-left characters, and if any are found, make sure that the whole string satisfies the requirements for bidirectional strings. If it does not, return an error.

These steps MUST be performed in the order given. The mappings and the optional normalization can be one-to-none, one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one or many-to-many, so the output of a step might be shorter or longer than the input, and the system using stringprep MUST be prepared to receive a longer or shorter string than the one input.

A profile of stringprep MUST include all of the following: the intended applicability of the profile; the character repertoire that is the input and output to stringprep, which is Unicode 3.2 for this version; the mapping tables used; any additional mapping tables specific to the profile; the Unicode normalization used, if any; the tables of characters prohibited as output; the bidirectional string testing used, if any; and any additional characters prohibited as output specific to the profile. Each profile MUST state the character repertoire it operates on, and each profile MUST be registered with IANA, with the IESG reviewing each profile. Protocol developers are strongly encouraged to look through the IANA profile registry when creating new profiles and to re-use logic from earlier profiles where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The order matters and is fixed. First rewrite or delete characters, then optionally put the result into a standard form, then reject anything that should not appear, then check that right-to-left text is not ambiguous. A protocol picks which of these it wants by naming a profile, and each profile names the tables it uses.

sections.title: Mapping: Deleting Characters and Folding Case
sections.content:
Some characters are simply deleted from the input, that is, mapped to nothing, because their presence or absence in protocol identifiers should not make two strings different. These fall into two groups. Some are only useful in line-based text and are otherwise invisible and ignored, such as the soft hyphen, the Mongolian todo soft hyphen, the zero width space, the word joiner and the zero width no-break space. Others affect glyph choice and glyph placement but do not bear semantics, such as the combining grapheme joiner, the zero width non-joiner and zero width joiner, and the variation selectors one through sixteen.

The second part of mapping is case folding. If a profile is going to map characters for case-insensitive comparison, that profile SHOULD map using either appendix B.2 or appendix B.3. Appendix B.2 is for profiles that also use Unicode normalization form KC, while appendix B.3 is for profiles that do not use Unicode normalization. These tables map from uppercase to lowercase characters. Note that this could have been done by changing all lowercase characters into uppercase, but the upper-to-lower folding was chosen because there is a tradition of using lowercase in current Internet applications and protocols.

If a profile creates its own mapping tables for case folding, they SHOULD be based on Unicode Technical Report 21 and SHOULD map from uppercase characters to lowercase, using the CaseFolding.txt file from the Unicode database, and the profile SHOULD do full case mapping, that is, using statuses C, F and I.

Authors of profiles need to consider the effects of changing the mapping of any currently assigned character when updating their profiles. Adding a new mapping for a currently assigned character, or changing an existing mapping, could cause a variance between the behaviour of systems that have been updated and systems that have not.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of character are thrown away. Some are invisible marks that exist only to change how a word is drawn. Others are there for the same reason but affect nothing at all. Separately, a profile that wants to ignore case folds upper case letters down to lower case.

sections.title: Normalization and Prohibited Output
sections.content:
The output of the mapping step is optionally normalized using one of the Unicode normalization forms. A profile can specify one of two options: no normalization, or Unicode normalization with form KC. A profile MAY choose to do no normalization, but such a profile can easily yield results that will be surprising to typical users, depending on the input mechanism they use. Some input mechanisms enter compatibility characters that look exactly like the underlying characters but have different code points. Another example is characters with multiple combining diacritics, where normalization orders those diacritics in a predictable fashion.

Unicode normalization requires fairly large tables and somewhat complicated character reordering logic, and that size and complexity should be weighed against the problems of user surprise from comparing unnormalized strings. The tables used for normalization are not given in this document but must be derived from the Unicode database.

There is a third form of normalization, form C. If a profile is going to use a Unicode normalization, it MUST use form KC. Form KC maps many compatibility characters to their equivalents, so using form KC instead of form C causes more strings that users would expect to match to actually match. A profile that specifies normalization MUST use the normalization associated with the version of the Unicode character set specified for the profile, and the composition process requires a fixed composition version of Unicode so that strings normalized under one version remain normalized under all future versions.

Before the text can be emitted, it MUST be checked for prohibited code points, and a profile MAY use all or some of the prohibition tables. The stringprep process never emits both an error and a string: if an error is detected during the checking for prohibited code points, only an error is returned. A profile MAY prohibit additional characters.

The tables cover nine categories. Space characters can make accurate visual transcription nearly impossible. Control characters cannot be seen and can cause unpredictable results when displayed. Private-use characters do not have defined meanings and are likely to be prohibited. Non-character code points are allocated in ISO/IEC 10646 but are not characters. Surrogate codes are permanently reserved for use as surrogate code values in the UTF-16 encoding and will never be assigned to characters. Characters that are inappropriate for plain text do not appear in regular text, including the replacement character, which renderers use to show that a character cannot be drawn. Characters that are inappropriate for canonical representation, the ideographic description characters, allow different sequences of characters to be rendered the same way. Characters that change display properties or are deprecated can change the order in which characters appear when rendered. Tagging characters are used for tagging text and are invisible.
sections.plainLanguage: Normalization puts text into one standard form, so that the same name typed two ways comes out identical. The prohibition tables then reject characters that would be invisible, would draw unpredictably, or would mean nothing: control characters, private-use characters, surrogates, and the marks that reorder text on screen.

sections.title: Bidirectional Text and Unassigned Code Points
sections.content:
Most characters are displayed from left to right, but some are displayed from right to left, and this feature of Unicode is called bidirectional text. All Unicode text is stored in logical order. A profile MAY choose to ignore bidirectional text, but ignoring it can cause display ambiguities: it is quite easy to create two different strings with the same characters in a different order that are correctly displayed identically. Profile creators should therefore strongly consider including the bidirectional character handling in their profile.

For the purposes of the requirements, a RandALCat character is one with Unicode bidirectional categories R or AL, and an LCat character is one with category L. Many characters fall in neither definition; Latin digits are an example, because they have category EN. In any profile that specifies bidirectional character handling, all three of the following requirements MUST be met. The characters that change display properties must be prohibited. If a string contains any RandALCat character, the string MUST NOT contain any LCat character. And if a string contains any RandALCat character, a RandALCat character MUST be the first character of the string and a RandALCat character MUST be the last.

The document then handles unassigned code points, and this is the only part where the rules for queries differ from those for stored strings. Stored strings are strings used in protocol identifiers and named entities, such as names in digital certificates and DNS domain name parts. Queries are strings matched against stored identifiers, such as user-entered names. All code points not assigned in the character repertoire named in a profile are called unassigned code points. Stored strings using the profile MUST NOT contain any unassigned code points, while queries for matching strings MAY contain them.

Using two different policies removes the need for versioning in protocols that use stringprep profiles, and makes the overall processing simpler without imposing a protocol to handle versioning. The list of unassigned code points MUST be given in a profile and MUST be used by implementations. The goal is to prevent comparisons between two strings that were both permitted to contain unassigned code points, because a negative result would not be definitive, and a positive result would not be definitive either.

Each code point in a repertoire is categorized by how it acts in the process: AO for code points that can be in the output, MN for those that can never appear as output from mapping or normalization, D for those disallowed in the prohibition step, and U for unassigned code points. A subsequent version of a profile that references a newer repertoire will inherently have some code points move from category U to AO, MN or D, and for backwards compatibility a subsequent version MUST NOT move code points from any other category. Stored strings MUST NOT contain any code points outside AO for the latest version of a profile, and applications creating queries MUST treat U code points as if they were AO.
sections.plainLanguage: Text in a right-to-left language is stored in the order it is read, but drawn in a different order, and that can make two different strings look identical. The rules here stop that from happening. They also handle code points that Unicode has not assigned yet: a name that is stored may not contain them, but a search for a name may, so that a new character can be searched for before every system has been updated.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are security considerations specific to stringprep, and others that are generic to using Unicode.

The Unicode and ISO/IEC 10646 repertoires have many characters that look similar. In many cases, users of security protocols might do visual matching, such as when comparing the names of trusted third parties. Because it is impossible to map similar-looking characters without a great deal of context such as knowing the fonts used, stringprep does nothing to map similar-looking characters together, nor to prohibit some characters because they look like others. User applications can help disambiguate some similar-looking characters by showing the user when a string changes between scripts.

Most profiles of stringprep can cause changes in strings that are input, so protocols that have sets of non-allowed characters or sequences MUST check for those after the stringprep processing. This document does not mandate the checking of bidirectional characters, and if those requirements are not used in a profile it is easy to create many strings whose characters are in a different order but are displayed identically, which can cause security-related user confusion similar to look-alike characters.

Stringprep does not do anything to assure that any algorithm translating characters from non-Unicode into Unicode produces the same output in all implementations. Some Unicode code points are invisible, and protocols that allow them can cause user confusion when two identical-looking strings do not match.

On the generic Unicode considerations: using Unicode characters explicitly forces applications to use multi-octet characters, and converting an application from single-octet to multi-octet characters must be done very carefully, particularly in an application that checks character values or sorts characters. Some applications do not check for illegal or ill-formed sequences in the encoding, and therefore fail to detect sequences of octets that would have been detected if they used just ASCII. All programs should reject any string that is an illegal or ill-formed octet sequence for the encoding being used. Both Unicode normalization and conversion between Unicode encodings can cause strings to grow or shrink, so programs that used fixed-size buffers are likely to fail in insecure fashions.

For IANA, stringprep profiles MUST have IETF consensus, each profile MUST be reviewed by the IESG before it is registered, and the IESG MAY change a profile before registration. The registry is a single text file with three fields per entry: the profile name, the RFC in which it is defined, and an indicator of whether it is the newest version. Each version of a profile remains listed forever, with the current-version indicator moved to the newer version. It is probably harmful if a large number of profiles proliferate, so the IESG may reject proposals for new profiles and suggest that protocols reuse existing ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The limits of this approach are worth knowing. It does not tell apart characters that merely look alike, so a name written with a different script can still pass as the same one, and a protocol that checks for forbidden sequences has to do that after the preparation step rather than before.

items.title: 1. Map
items.text: Replace each character with its mapping, or delete it if it maps to nothing. Mapped characters are not checked again.

items.title: 2. Normalize
items.text: Optionally put the result into Unicode form KC, or leave it alone.

items.title: 3. Prohibit
items.text: Reject any character the profile forbids. An error replaces the output.

items.title: 4. Check bidi
items.text: If right-to-left characters are present, check the whole string against the bidi rules.

viz.caption: THE FOUR CATEGORIES OF CODE POINT IN A PROFILE

items.label: Assignable output
items.desc: Code points that can be in the output.

items.label: Mapped away
items.desc: Code points that can never appear as output from mapping or normalization.

items.label: Disallowed
items.desc: Code points that cannot be in the output because the prohibition step disallows them.

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: Code points not yet assigned in the repertoire. Forbidden in stored strings, allowed in queries.
